title: Learning in intervals
text: Two students study the same vocabulary list for the same total of {{1}}. One does it all in a single evening; the other spreads the same time over a fortnight of short sessions. When tested later, the second student remembers {{2}} more — one of the most replicated findings in the psychology of learning. The spacing effect was first {{3}} in the 1880s, and it survives every attempt to make it disappear. The reason lies in how memory {{4}}: a skill practised just as it begins to fade gets {{5}} back into long-term storage, and the slight effort of retrieval is precisely what strengthens it. Massed practice — the familiar all-nighter — keeps the material feeling fluent, which is exactly why it {{6}}: fluency in the moment is not durability over time. The principle now {{7}} behind a thousand app icons: flashcard programs schedule each item for review at the moment you are about to forget it, squeezing maximum retention from minimum minutes. Teachers can apply the same logic offline by {{8}} last month's material into this month's lessons. The message is liberating: forgetting is not failure but part of the mechanism — each near-miss is the workout that memory needs.

gaps.explanation: 'the same total of hours' — time spent; horde = a crowd, hunch = a suspicion.
'remembers far more' — 'far' intensifies comparatives; 'fairly more' and 'fast more' are not grammatical.
'first documented in the 1880s' — written down and reported; detonate = explode, dominate = control.
'lies in how memory works' — operates; the other verbs are possible with objects but nonsense about memory here.
'gets locked back into long-term storage' — secured there; loom = appear large and threatening, loop = form a circle.
'which is exactly why it fails' — does not deliver lasting results; fell = knock down, foil = thwart someone else.
'the principle now sits behind a thousand app icons' — resides there; split = divide in two.
'by weaving last month's material into this month's lessons' — threading it in; wade = walk through water, wave = move a hand.
